parts.title: Reporting a lost bag

turns.text: Good morning, Lakeside Transit lost and found. This is Ray Donnelly speaking. How can I help you?
turns.speaker: clerk

turns.text: Hi, yes. I left my bag on one of your buses this week, and I'm really hoping somebody handed it in. I've already looked everywhere at home, just in case.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Okay, let's see what we can do. I'll start a report for you first. Can I get your name, please?
turns.speaker: clerk

turns.text: Sure. It's Paula Kessler.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.say: Is that K, E, S, L, E, R?
turns.text: Is that K-E-S-L-E-R?
turns.speaker: clerk

turns.say: Almost. There are two S's. Kessler, K, E, S, S, L, E, R.
turns.text: Almost. There are two S's. Kessler, K-E-S-S-L-E-R.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Got it, thanks. And which bus were you on?
turns.speaker: clerk

turns.text: It was the number 74. Oh, wait, no, sorry. The 74 is the one I take home. I was on the 47, the one that runs downtown.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: The 47, okay. And what day was that?
turns.speaker: clerk

turns.text: I was going to say Monday, because I had a dentist appointment that day, but they moved it. So it was Tuesday, around four in the afternoon.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Tuesday, around four. Do you remember where you got off?
turns.speaker: clerk

turns.say: Yes, I got on at Main Street and got off at the stop on Carlton Avenue, right by the hospital. That's C, A, R, L, T, O, N.
turns.text: Yes, I got on at Main Street and got off at the stop on Carlton Avenue, right by the hospital. That's C-A-R-L-T-O-N.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Great. Now, can you describe the bag for me?
turns.speaker: clerk

turns.text: It's a backpack, medium size. It looks kind of gray in some light, but it's actually dark green.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Dark green. And what's it made of? Is it leather, or nylon, or something else?
turns.speaker: clerk

turns.text: Not leather, no. It's canvas, the thick kind. It's a little worn at the bottom.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Is there anything that would help us recognize it? We get a lot of backpacks in here, and many of them look the same.
turns.speaker: clerk

turns.text: Well, there used to be a keychain on the zipper, but that fell off months ago. Oh, but there's a flag sewn onto the front pocket. A small Canadian one. My sister brought it back from Toronto.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: That's really helpful. Okay, and what was inside the bag?
turns.speaker: clerk

turns.text: Let me think. A water bottle, a couple of magazines, some snacks. My wallet isn't in there, thank goodness. I keep that in my coat. But my camera is, and that's what I'm really worried about. It was a birthday present.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: I understand. We'll do our best. Now, what's the best number to reach you on?
turns.speaker: clerk

turns.say: My home number is seven seven three, five five five, zero one two nine, but honestly, I'm hardly ever there. You'd better call my cell. That's seven seven three, five five five, zero one eight six.
turns.text: My home number is 773 555 0129, but honestly, I'm hardly ever there. You'd better call my cell. That's 773 555 0186.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.say: Let me read that back. seven seven three, five five five, zero one eight six.
turns.text: Let me read that back. 773 555 0186.
turns.speaker: clerk

turns.text: That's right.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Okay. I've checked our system, and nothing matching your bag has been logged yet. But items from the buses don't always reach us right away. Sometimes it takes two or three days, so please don't worry yet.
turns.speaker: clerk

turns.text: Oh, okay. And how long do you hold on to things?
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: We used to keep everything for 60 days, but the policy changed last year. Now it's 30 days. After that, items go to charity.
turns.speaker: clerk

turns.text: Okay, good to know. And would I pick it up at the main bus station?
turns.speaker: caller

turns.say: No, a lot of people go there by mistake. Our lost property office is at 215 Harmon Street. That's H, A, R, M, O, N. It's open weekdays from eight to six, and you'll need to bring some photo ID.
turns.text: No, a lot of people go there by mistake. Our lost property office is at 215 Harmon Street. That's H-A-R-M-O-N. It's open weekdays from eight to six, and you'll need to bring some photo ID.
turns.speaker: clerk

turns.text: Okay. Is there a charge for that?
turns.speaker: caller

turns.say: If you pick it up yourself, there's a handling fee of five dollars. We can also send it to your home, but that costs twelve dollars, because of the delivery.
turns.text: If you pick it up yourself, there's a handling fee of $5. We can also send it to your home, but that costs $12, because of the delivery.
turns.speaker: clerk

turns.text: Oh, I'll just come in. It's not far from my office.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: Sounds good. As soon as your bag shows up, we'll give you a call on your cell.
turns.speaker: clerk

turns.text: Thank you so much. You've been really helpful.
turns.speaker: caller

turns.text: You're welcome, Ms. Kessler. Have a good day.
turns.speaker: clerk

groups.title: Lost Property Report

questions.prompt: Caller's surname: ______
questions.evidence: There are two S's. Kessler, K-E-S-S-L-E-R.

explanation.en: The clerk spells the name with one S, but the caller corrects him: there are two S's, so it is Kessler.
explanation.ru: Сотрудник записывает фамилию с одной "S", но звонящая его поправляет: там две "S", то есть "Kessler".
explanation.uk: Співробітник записує прізвище з однією "S", але жінка, яка телефонує, його виправляє: там дві "S", тобто "Kessler".

questions.prompt: Bus route number: ______
questions.evidence: I was on the 47, the one that runs downtown.

explanation.en: She first says 74, but corrects herself: the 74 is her bus home, and she was on the 47.
explanation.ru: Сначала она говорит "74", но тут же поправляется: "74" — это автобус, на котором она ездит домой, а ехала она на "47".
explanation.uk: Спочатку вона каже "74", але одразу виправляється: "74" — це автобус, яким вона їздить додому, а їхала вона "47".

questions.prompt: Day of journey: ______
questions.evidence: So it was Tuesday, around four in the afternoon.

explanation.en: She almost says Monday, but her dentist appointment was moved, so the journey was on Tuesday.
explanation.ru: Она чуть не говорит "Monday", но её запись к стоматологу перенесли, поэтому поездка была во вторник — "Tuesday".
explanation.uk: Вона мало не каже "Monday", але її візит до стоматолога перенесли, тож поїздка була у вівторок — "Tuesday".

questions.prompt: Got off at: ______ Avenue
questions.evidence: got off at the stop on Carlton Avenue, right by the hospital. That's C-A-R-L-T-O-N.

explanation.en: She got on at Main Street but got off on Carlton Avenue, which she spells.
explanation.ru: Она села на "Main Street", а вышла на "Carlton Avenue" и продиктовала это название по буквам.
explanation.uk: Вона сіла на "Main Street", а вийшла на "Carlton Avenue" і продиктувала цю назву по літерах.

questions.prompt: Color: dark ______
questions.evidence: but it's actually dark green.

explanation.en: The bag can look gray in some light, but she says it is really dark green.
explanation.ru: При некотором освещении сумка может казаться серой ("gray"), но, по её словам, на самом деле она тёмно-зелёная — "dark green".
explanation.uk: За певного освітлення сумка може здаватися сірою ("gray"), але, за її словами, насправді вона темно-зелена — "dark green".

questions.prompt: Material: ______
questions.evidence: It's canvas, the thick kind.

explanation.en: The clerk suggests leather or nylon, but she says it is not leather; it is canvas.
explanation.ru: Сотрудник предполагает кожу ("leather") или нейлон ("nylon"), но она говорит, что сумка не кожаная, а из парусины — "canvas".
explanation.uk: Співробітник припускає шкіру ("leather") або нейлон ("nylon"), але вона каже, що сумка не шкіряна, а з парусини — "canvas".

explanation.uk: Гаманця ("wallet") у сумці немає: вона тримає його в пальті ("coat"). Хвилюється вона за фотоапарат — "camera", який їй подарували на день народження.

questions.evidence: You'd better call my cell. That's 773 555 0186.

explanation.en: She gives her home number first, ending 0129, but says she is hardly ever home, so the clerk should use her cell number, ending 0186.
explanation.ru: Сначала она называет домашний номер, который заканчивается на "0129", но говорит, что почти не бывает дома, поэтому сотруднику лучше звонить на мобильный, который заканчивается на "0186".
explanation.uk: Спочатку вона називає домашній номер, що закінчується на "0129", але каже, що майже не буває вдома, тож співробітникові краще телефонувати на мобільний, який закінчується на "0186".

questions.prompt: Found items are kept for ______ days
questions.evidence: Now it's 30 days.

explanation.en: Items used to be kept for 60 days, but the policy changed, and now they are kept for 30 days.
explanation.ru: Раньше вещи хранили "60" дней, но правила изменились, и теперь их хранят "30" дней.
explanation.uk: Раніше речі зберігали "60" днів, але правила змінилися, і тепер їх зберігають "30" днів.

questions.prompt: Lost property office: 215 ______ Street
questions.evidence: Our lost property office is at 215 Harmon Street. That's H-A-R-M-O-N.

explanation.en: The office is not at the main bus station. It is on Harmon Street, which the clerk spells.
explanation.ru: Бюро находок находится не на главном автовокзале, а на "Harmon Street" — сотрудник диктует это название по буквам.
explanation.uk: Бюро знахідок розташоване не на головному автовокзалі, а на "Harmon Street" — співробітник диктує цю назву по літерах.

parts.title: Welcome to Wattle Creek Wildlife Sanctuary

turns.text: G'day, everyone, and welcome to Wattle Creek Wildlife Sanctuary. My name's Brett Kinsella, and I'm one of the guides here. Before you head off, I'll give you a quick idea of where everything is, and then I'll run through today's talks and feeding times. So grab one of our maps and have it handy.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Right. So you've just come in through the main gate, and you're at the bottom of the main path, which runs north through the middle of the sanctuary. On your left is the Visitor Centre, where you bought your tickets, and that's also where you'll find the toilets and the gift shop. A lot of people go looking for food in there, but the café's actually directly across from it, on the right-hand side of the path as you come in. It does good coffee, and the sausage rolls are excellent.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Okay, now walk north up the main path. Just past the Visitor Centre, there's another building on your left, right on the corner where our two paths cross. That's the reptile house. It's air-conditioned, so it's a good place to cool down if it gets hot this arvo.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Keep going straight over the crossroads and right to the end of the main path, and that's where you'll find the koalas. You'll notice the eucalyptus grove up in the north-west corner, and some visitors expect to see koalas in there. But that's just where we grow the leaves we feed them, so don't waste your time looking up in those trees.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Now, come back down to the crossroads and turn right, so you're heading east along the cross path. The first building on your left is the aviary, with our parrots and cockatoos. Behind it, further north, there's a smaller building, and that's the nocturnal house, where you can see bilbies and possums. It's kept dark inside, so give your eyes a minute to adjust.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: On the opposite side of the cross path, the south side, there's a grassy area right on the corner of the main path, with the lake just to the east of it. That's the picnic area. There are tables and barbecues, and you're welcome to bring your own lunch. Just keep an eye on your sandwiches, because the ducks from the lake are very bold.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Okay, last bit of the map. Go back to the crossroads and this time head west, past the reptile house. Right at the far end of the path, on your left, you'll find the wombat burrows. They dig all day, so you might only see the tops of their heads.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Now, on the other side of the path, opposite the wombats, there's a big open field, just south of the eucalyptus grove. That's the kangaroo paddock, and you're allowed to walk right in among them. They're very relaxed.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Right, now for today's programme. The koala talk is usually at 11 o'clock, but today it's been pushed back half an hour, to 11:30, because the keeper's had to take one of the joeys to the vet. Nothing serious, I'm told. It runs for about thirty minutes, so you'll be finished by 12, in time for lunch.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: At one o'clock there's the reptile talk, in the reptile house. Visitors used to be able to hold one of our pythons, but we stopped that last year, sorry. What you can do is give one of our blue-tongue lizards a gentle stroke. People sometimes ask about feeding the turtles too, but only the keepers are allowed to do that.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.say: Then at two o'clock, sorry, quarter past two, the keepers feed the kangaroos, and you can join in. Please don't give them bread or anything you've brought from home, because it makes them sick. You'll need one of our special feed bags, which are three dollars each from the Visitor Centre. Not the café, by the way. They don't sell them there.
turns.text: Then at two o'clock, sorry, quarter past two, the keepers feed the kangaroos, and you can join in. Please don't give them bread or anything you've brought from home, because it makes them sick. You'll need one of our special feed bags, which are $3 each from the Visitor Centre. Not the café, by the way. They don't sell them there.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Normally at three o'clock we'd have the free-flight bird show near the aviary, but I'm afraid it's off today. It's a bit windy, but that's not the reason, the birds are fine with a breeze, and they're all perfectly healthy. It's because workers are fixing the aviary roof this afternoon, and the noise would upset them.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Finally, the wombat feeding is at quarter to four, at the burrows. There's no seating there, so it's standing room only, and please, no flash photography, as it frightens them. My advice is to get there about ten minutes before it starts, because the viewing area fills up quickly.
turns.speaker: guide

turns.text: Okay, that's it from me. If you've got any questions, just look for me or any of the staff in green shirts. Enjoy your day!
turns.speaker: guide

questions.prompt: Café
questions.evidence: the café's actually directly across from it, on the right-hand side of the path as you come in

explanation.en: The café is opposite the Visitor Centre, on the right as you walk in from the main gate. Many people look for food in the Visitor Centre, but it is not there.
explanation.ru: Кафе находится напротив "Visitor Centre", справа, если входить через главные ворота. Многие ищут еду в "Visitor Centre", но её там нет.
explanation.uk: Кафе розташоване навпроти "Visitor Centre", праворуч, якщо заходити через головну браму. Багато хто шукає їжу у "Visitor Centre", але там її немає.

questions.prompt: Reptile house
questions.evidence: Just past the Visitor Centre, there's another building on your left, right on the corner where our two paths cross. That's the reptile house.

explanation.en: Walking north, the reptile house is the next building on the left after the Visitor Centre, at the corner where the paths cross.
explanation.ru: Если идти на север, террариум — следующее здание слева после "Visitor Centre", на углу, где пересекаются дорожки.
explanation.uk: Якщо йти на північ, тераріум — наступна будівля ліворуч після "Visitor Centre", на розі, де перетинаються доріжки.

questions.prompt: Koala enclosure
questions.evidence: right to the end of the main path, and that's where you'll find the koalas

explanation.en: The koalas are at the very end of the main path. They are not in the eucalyptus grove, which is only where their food is grown.
explanation.ru: Коалы — в самом конце главной дорожки. Они не в эвкалиптовой роще: там только выращивают для них корм.
explanation.uk: Коали — у самому кінці головної доріжки. Вони не в евкаліптовому гаю: там лише вирощують для них корм.

questions.prompt: Aviary
questions.evidence: turn right, so you're heading east along the cross path. The first building on your left is the aviary

explanation.en: Turning right at the crossroads means walking east, and the aviary is the first building on the left (north side). The building behind it is the nocturnal house.
explanation.ru: Повернуть направо на перекрёстке — значит идти на восток, и вольер для птиц — первое здание слева (с северной стороны). Здание за ним — павильон ночных животных.
explanation.uk: Повернути праворуч на перехресті — означає йти на схід, і пташиний вольєр — перша будівля ліворуч (з північного боку). Будівля за ним — павільйон нічних тварин.

questions.prompt: Picnic area
questions.evidence: there's a grassy area right on the corner of the main path, with the lake just to the east of it. That's the picnic area.

explanation.en: The picnic area is on the south side of the cross path, at the corner with the main path, with the lake to its east.
explanation.ru: Зона для пикника находится к югу от поперечной дорожки, на углу с главной дорожкой; к востоку от неё — озеро.
explanation.uk: Зона для пікніка розташована з південного боку поперечної доріжки, на розі з головною доріжкою; на схід від неї — озеро.

questions.prompt: Wombat burrows
questions.evidence: head west, past the reptile house. Right at the far end of the path, on your left, you'll find the wombat burrows

explanation.en: Walking west past the reptile house, the wombat burrows are at the far end of the path on the left (south side).
explanation.ru: Если идти на запад мимо террариума, норы вомбатов — в дальнем конце дорожки слева (с южной стороны).
explanation.uk: Якщо йти на захід повз тераріум, нори вомбатів — у дальньому кінці доріжки ліворуч (з південного боку).

parts.title: Sleep and exam performance

turns.text: Okay, Holly, shall we get going on this presentation? We've got fifteen minutes on sleep and exam performance, and we need to send the tutor an outline by Friday.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Yeah, sounds good. Before we get into the individual studies, though, can I just say what surprised me in the background reading? I'd assumed students would have a fair idea of how much they sleep, but apparently most of them reckon they get far more than they really do.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Mm, I noticed that too. And I'd always been told naps were a bad idea, that they ruin your sleep at night.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Same here, but the reading said a short nap's fine, and that didn't really surprise me, because my flatmate swears by them. No, the thing that got me was how long one bad night lasts. You miss a single night's sleep and your memory still isn't back to normal three days later.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Yeah, that's quite something. I wasn't surprised that nearly all the research was done on university students rather than school kids, though. I suppose they're easy to recruit.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: True. And did anything about the research itself bother you?
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Well, a lot of it depends on students saying how long they slept. Nobody actually measured it. They just filled in a questionnaire afterwards.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Right, and given what we just said about people overestimating, that's a real weakness. I thought the samples might be tiny too, but most had several hundred participants, so that's fine.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: And they're mostly from the last ten years, so they're not out of date.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: No. But what none of them seemed to ask about was paid work. Heaps of students do evening shifts in cafés or bars, and that's bound to affect both their sleep and their marks.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: How long is it?
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Exactly. What if we kick off by asking everyone how many hours they slept last night? Just a show of hands. It gets them involved straight away.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: I like that. We could also run a quick memory test with the audience, you know, read out a list of words.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: Hmm, I think that's risky. It might not work with a tired class at nine in the morning. Let's keep it simple.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Fair enough. Should we split the speaking fifty-fifty?
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Great. Right, the studies themselves. Let's go through them and check we agree on what each one found. First, the Auckland study of first-year students.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.text: That's the one comparing students who went to bed around the same time every night with those whose bedtimes were all over the place. The regular group ended up with better marks, even though the total hours they slept were about the same.
turns.speaker: student_a

turns.text: Then there's the study of trainee nurses. They were tested after a night shift. Their memory for patient details was actually fine, but they made far more mistakes when working out drug doses.
turns.speaker: student_b

turns.speaker: student_a

parts.title: The history of papermaking

turns.text: Good morning, everyone. I'm Dr Edward Lockwood, and today we're continuing our series on everyday technologies with something you probably take for granted: paper. I'll begin with how it was first made, then look at how the craft spread westwards, and I'll finish with the machines of the nineteenth century and recycling today.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Right. Before paper, people wrote on all sorts of surfaces. The Egyptians used papyrus, which is where our word 'paper' comes from, and in China people wrote on strips of bamboo or on silk. The trouble was that bamboo was heavy and silk was very expensive, so there was a real need for something better.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: The traditional date for the invention of paper is the year 105, when a court official called Cai Lun presented the process to the emperor. Archaeologists have since found older fragments, so he probably improved the method rather than inventing it. Let's go through the process step by step, as it was carried out in his time.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: First, the raw materials were collected: the inner bark of the mulberry tree, hemp, old rags and even worn-out fishing nets. These were chopped into small pieces and left to soak in water. Now, you might expect salt to be added at this point, but in fact what they added was lime, which helped to break the material down.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Next, the softened material was beaten with wooden hammers. This was hard, tiring work, and it could go on for hours, until the fibres separated and formed a thick pulp. That was mixed with plenty of water in a large vat. Then came the clever part. The papermaker dipped a screen into the vat and lifted it out, covered in a thin layer of fibres. The earliest screens were made of cloth, but cloth tended to sag, so they soon switched to bamboo, which kept the sheet perfectly flat.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: The water drained away through the screen, and the wet sheet was pressed to squeeze out the rest. Some workshops hung their sheets on lines, rather like washing, but the usual method was to brush each one onto a heated wall, where it dried in just a few minutes. And the last stage? Once it was completely dry, the sheet was polished with a smooth stone, so that ink wouldn't spread across it. Some makers tried shells for this, but stone gave a better finish.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: OK, so how did this knowledge leave China? For several centuries it was kept fairly secret. The usual story is that it reached Samarkand, in Central Asia, in 751, after a battle in which Chinese papermakers were taken prisoner. Samarkand had clean rivers, but plenty of towns had those. What really made it successful was the flax grown all around the city, which gave a steady supply of fibre.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: From there, the craft moved to Baghdad, where a paper mill was working by the 790s. Government offices were quick to adopt it. Until then, official records had been kept on parchment, made from animal skin, and paper replaced it partly because it was cheaper, but mainly because anything scraped off paper left a visible mark, so documents were much harder to forge.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Papermaking then crossed North Africa and reached Spain in the twelfth century, and Italy shortly afterwards. The Italian mills, especially in a town called Fabriano, made several improvements. They used animal glue to give the paper a harder surface, which is interesting, but the innovation I'd like you to note down is the watermark. These were faint designs pressed into each sheet, so that buyers could tell which mill had produced it.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Right, let's jump to the nineteenth century. By around 1800, demand was growing fast because of newspapers and the spread of schooling, but European paper was still made from rags, and there simply weren't enough of them to go round. Some mills even put up notices asking households to save their old clothes.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Hand production was also slow. A skilled team might manage a few thousand sheets a day. The answer was the machine developed in England by the Fourdrinier brothers and patented in 1806. Instead of producing separate sheets, it made paper as one continuous roll, which could then be cut to whatever size the customer wanted.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: That still left the problem of raw materials. From the 1840s, the solution was wood pulp, which was cheap and almost unlimited. But this new paper had a serious flaw. It contained acid from the production process, and over time that acid makes paper turn yellow and brittle. British libraries now spend millions of pounds trying to rescue books from this period, while much older rag paper is often in far better condition.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: Finally, recycling. A lot of people believe paper can be recycled forever, but it can't. Each time it goes through the process, the fibres get shorter and weaker. You'll see figures of five times quoted, but most experts put the limit at around seven, after which the fibres are too short to bond together.
turns.speaker: lecturer

turns.text: People also worry about ink, but that's actually removed quite easily, using soap and air bubbles that carry it to the surface. The real headache for recycling plants is grease from things like takeaway pizza boxes, because it can't be separated from the fibres, and it ruins a whole batch. Next week, we'll look at printing.
turns.speaker: lecturer
